reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: RPGN is a nephrological emergency defined by a rapid loss of renal function over days to weeks, accompanied by a nephritic urine sediment with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
The histological hallmark is crescent formation in a large proportion of glomeruli, reflecting severe glomerular injury and rupture of capillary walls
It is classified into three immunopathological groups: anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, immune-complex-mediated disease, and pauci-immune (usually ANCA-associated) disease
Coexisting pulmonary haemorrhage with glomerulonephritis (pulmonary-renal syndrome) suggests anti-GBM disease or ANCA-associated vasculitis and demands urgent evaluation
Early kidney biopsy is central to diagnosis and to gauging the balance of active (treatable) crescents versus fibrous (irreversible) scarring
Serological testing for ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, complement levels, and other markers helps categorise the disease and guide treatment
Outcome depends critically on how quickly immunosuppression is started, since delay allows crescents to organise into irreversible fibrosis
Management principles centre on prompt aggressive immunosuppression, with plasma exchange added in anti-GBM disease and in selected severe or dialysis-dependent vasculitis cases
reference.pathophysiology: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis describes a clinical syndrome of accelerating renal failure caused by severe inflammatory glomerular injury, characterised pathologically by extensive crescents. Crescents form when damage to the glomerular capillary wall allows plasma proteins, fibrin, and inflammatory cells to enter Bowman space, where proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages compress the glomerular tuft. Three mechanisms underlie the syndrome: linear deposition of antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM disease), deposition of immune complexes as seen in lupus, post-infectious, and IgA-related disease, and a pauci-immune process typically associated with ANCA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis. In all forms, unchecked inflammation rapidly destroys glomeruli and, without timely treatment, progresses to fibrous scarring and end-stage kidney disease.
additionalInvestigations: Urine microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
Kidney biopsy for crescent quantification and immunofluorescence pattern
ANCA testing (including antigen-specific assays) and anti-GBM antibody titres
Complement levels and other autoimmune serologies including antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies
Chest imaging when pulmonary haemorrhage is suspected
Quantification of proteinuria and serial renal function monitoring
redFlags: Pulmonary haemorrhage with haemoptysis and hypoxaemia indicating a pulmonary-renal syndrome
Rapidly rising creatinine or oliguria threatening imminent dialysis dependence
Systemic vasculitic features such as mononeuritis, purpura, or ENT involvement
reference.prognosis: Untreated RPGN progresses to end-stage kidney disease within weeks. With early immunosuppression many patients recover useful renal function, but prognosis worsens sharply with delayed treatment, a high proportion of fibrous crescents, dialysis dependence at presentation, and anti-GBM disease with advanced injury. Relapse is common in ANCA-associated disease and requires ongoing surveillance.
pitfalls: Delaying biopsy and treatment while awaiting serology, allowing crescents to become irreversible
Missing coexisting pulmonary haemorrhage that changes urgency and management
Assuming a negative ANCA excludes vasculitis, since a minority are seronegative
Starting heavy immunosuppression in a kidney already dominated by fibrous scarring with little chance of recovery
management: Urgent immunosuppression with high-dose corticosteroids combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab to arrest crescentic injury
Plasma exchange for anti-GBM disease and for ANCA-associated disease with pulmonary haemorrhage or severe renal failure
Renal replacement therapy for established kidney failure, alongside general supportive measures and blood-pressure control
Directed treatment of the underlying process, such as lupus nephritis or a post-infectious cause, guided by early biopsy and serology
Maintenance immunosuppression with monitoring for relapse and for treatment-related infection, including prophylaxis against Pneumocystis
Immediate nephrology referral, as delayed treatment leads to irreversible end-stage kidney disease
